description: Which order minimum applies to an outlet, and whether an order meets it. The only business rule in the Order module with no server-side gate — the device is where it can still be acted on, so nothing downstream will catch a divergence between the two engines. Amounts are strings, per ../README.md; the tiebreak is the higher id compared as lowercase canonical strings, per the ordering note there.

resolution.name: no candidates is no minimum, and that is an answer
resolution.why: BR-ORD-5 says a minimum applies *if configured*, and most tenants configure none. A resolver that always returned something would pass a file of positive cases only.

resolution.name: a single channel minimum is the answer
an outlet minimum beats a channel one
resolution.why: B1's 'per channel/outlet' read the way BR-PRD-2 reads it. The channel row is listed second so a resolver that simply keeps the last candidate fails.

resolution.name: the more specific scope wins even when it asks for less
resolution.why: Specificity, not size. A resolver that took the larger amount would pass the case above by accident, because the outlet row happened to be smaller there too — it is smaller here as well, so this pins the direction rather than the magnitude.

resolution.name: a tie at one scope goes to the higher id
resolution.why: Two minimums at one scope is a data problem no tiebreak makes right. What it buys is that the server and every device refuse the same order — see the ordering note in ../README.md, including the `Guid.ToByteArray()` trap this pair is chosen to catch.

resolution.name: an id in upper case sorts by the same rule as one in lower
resolution.why: In ASCII 'A'-'F' sort below 'a'-'f', so an implementation comparing raw strings would let the winner depend on how somebody typed a GUID. Both engines lower-case first.

check.name: no minimum passes any order
check.why: The ordinary case. Every order was submittable at any value before BR-ORD-5 existed, and still is where nobody configured a minimum.

check.name: exactly the threshold is met
check.why: `>=`, not `>`. A rep who hits the number exactly has met it, and an off-by-one here refuses an order for a hundredth of a leu.

check.name: a hundredth under is not met
trailing zeros do not change the comparison
check.why: '500.00' and '500' are the same number and a decimal engine has to say so. A string comparison would call this NotMet.

check.name: different currencies is a refusal to answer, not a refusal of the order
check.why: Comparing 50 EUR against 200 RON by their numbers alone would refuse orders comfortably over the intended threshold and accept ones under it — and it would look like the rule working. A rep told 'your order is too small' about a misconfiguration adds stock nobody asked for and is still refused.

check.name: currency is matched without regard to case
check.why: The write path upper-cases what it stores, so this can only differ if some other path does not. Pinned because the failure would look like a misconfiguration to whoever hit it.

check.name: a stored amount that is not a decimal is a broken row, not a small order
check.why: Its own answer rather than borrowing the currency one: telling a rep their currencies disagree would send them looking for the wrong thing.

check.name: a thousands separator is unreadable rather than a thousand times larger
check.why: The failure both engines were written to avoid, from opposite directions: .NET has to *exclude* NumberStyles.AllowThousands, and decimal.js throws. A minimum a tenant meant as one and a half must not silently become fifteen hundred.

check.name: exponent notation is unreadable, because the write path would never have stored it
check.why: The case this file was worth writing for. .NET parses with AllowDecimalPoint|AllowLeadingSign, which excludes AllowExponent, so '1e2' is a broken row; decimal.js reads it as 100 and the device would have called a 100-leu order Met against a minimum the server cannot even read. Unreachable through the write path today — which is exactly the kind of assumption a vector file exists to stop depending on.

check.name: a hexadecimal amount is unreadable for the same reason
check.why: The second half of the same divergence. decimal.js reads '0x10' as 16; .NET reads it as nothing.

check.name: surrounding whitespace is unreadable
check.why: Neither engine trims, and they agree here already. Pinned because trimming is the obvious 'helpful' change somebody makes to one side.

check.name: a leading plus is an ordinary amount
check.why: The other side of the strictness: AllowLeadingSign is *in* the .NET style, and decimal.js takes it too. A regex written to reject exponents must not reject this.

check.name: an amount with no integer part is an ordinary amount
check.why: '.50' is legal to both engines. Listed for the same reason as the case above — the strictness has a shape, and this is one of its edges.

check.name: a non-finite amount is unreadable
check.why: The pair decimal.js accepts and .NET does not. `isFinite` is what catches it on the device.
